questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend catching specific exception types instead of a bare `except:`?
options: There is no difference between the two approaches
Specific exceptions run slower than catching everything
Python doesn't allow catching specific exception types
A bare except: hides real bugs along with the expected failures you meant to catch
questions.explain: Catching everything blindly can mask genuine bugs that should be visible, not silently swallowed.

questions.q: What do PyTorch and TensorFlow have in common, according to this lesson?
options: They were both discontinued in favor of newer tools
They're the two frameworks behind nearly every modern AI model, and both are Python libraries at their core
Neither one supports Python at all
They are competing programming languages, not libraries
questions.explain: Both are Python libraries, and together they underlie most modern AI model training.

questions.q: What's the practical difference between `import json` and `from json import loads`?
options: from json import loads is invalid Python syntax
import json only works with third-party packages, never the standard library
There is no difference — they behave identically in every case
The first requires prefixing with json. (like json.loads), while the second pulls loads directly into your namespace with no prefix
questions.explain: import json requires the json. prefix on every use; from json import loads lets you call loads() directly.

questions.q: Why does this lesson call dictionaries one of the most important structures for AI work?
options: Because dictionaries run faster than every other data type
Because AI APIs never return lists, only dictionaries
Because dictionaries are the only structure Python supports
Because every AI API response is JSON, and Python turns JSON directly into a dictionary
questions.explain: The lesson's core point is that JSON responses from AI APIs become Python dictionaries via json.loads().

questions.q: Given `models = ["gpt-4o", "claude-opus", "gemini-pro"]`, what does `models[-1]` return?
options: An error, since negative indices are not valid in Python
The entire list reversed
"gpt-4o" — the first item
"gemini-pro" — negative indices count from the end of the list
questions.explain: Negative indexing counts from the end, so -1 always refers to the last item.

questions.q: Which structure would you reach for to automatically remove duplicate values from a list of model names?
options: There is no structure in Python that handles this
A dictionary, since dictionaries cannot contain duplicates
A set — converting the list with set(my_list) drops duplicates automatically
A tuple, since tuples cannot contain duplicates
questions.explain: Converting a list to a set is the standard, idiomatic way to de-duplicate its values in Python.

questions.q: Why do AI SDKs ask you to construct a client object once (with your API key) instead of passing the API key to every individual function call?
options: It's required by Python syntax rules
It avoids repeating credentials and config on every call — the client stores them once via __init__ and self
It makes the API key get sent in plain text
It prevents the SDK from making more than one request
questions.explain: This is the same __init__/self pattern from Lesson 13: the client object stores credentials and config as instance attributes once, and every method call afterward reuses that stored state.

questions.q: When is `__init__` called?
options: Only when you call it explicitly, like any other method
Automatically, every time a new instance of the class is created
Only once per program, no matter how many instances are created
Only when the object is deleted
questions.explain: Python automatically calls `__init__` right after building a new instance, which is where you typically set up that instance's starting attributes.

questions.q: Why does `ask()` return an `AIResponse` dataclass instance instead of just a plain string?
options: A dataclass runs measurably faster than returning a string
Python requires every method to return a dataclass
It keeps the door open for more structured fields (like token counts) later, without breaking code that already uses response.text
Strings cannot be returned from instance methods
questions.explain: A structured return value can grow new fields over time while existing calling code (which only reads response.text) keeps working unchanged — the same reasoning real SDK response objects follow.

questions.q: A teammate says 'I installed the package, but my script still can't import it.' What's the most likely cause, based on this lesson?
options: Python itself is broken and needs reinstalling
The virtual environment was never activated (or a different one got activated), so the install and the running script are using different Python environments
pip only works on Linux
The package name must always match the import name exactly, with no exceptions
questions.explain: This is the classic venv mix-up: if the environment isn't active (or the wrong one is), pip install and your running script end up pointing at two different Python installations with two different sets of packages.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the most effective way to prevent most dependency conflicts from ever happening?
options: Never install more than one package total
Install every package with --no-deps
Only use packages with no dependencies of their own
Give each project (or each genuinely incompatible pair of tools) its own isolated virtual environment, rather than sharing one environment for everything
questions.explain: Most dependency conflicts arise from crowding unrelated tools into one shared environment. Isolating projects into separate virtual environments (Lesson 18) sidesteps the vast majority of these conflicts before they occur.

questions.q: Why does this course dedicate Chapter 5 specifically to the `requests` library rather than jumping straight to a provider SDK?
options: Because requests is the only library Python has
Because understanding raw HTTP, which requests handles, is what makes every provider SDK's behavior predictable instead of feeling like magic
Because provider SDKs don't actually use HTTP at all
Because requests is required to create a virtual environment
questions.explain: Every provider SDK is, underneath, making HTTP requests. Learning requests directly demystifies what those SDKs are actually doing on your behalf.

questions.q: Why is hardcoding an API key directly into a Python source file a serious problem, even if the repository is private?
options: It isn't a problem as long as the repo is private
Python cannot run code containing string literals
Once committed, the key remains in the git history even after the line is deleted, and rotating the key becomes the only real fix
It only matters if the file is named .env
questions.explain: Git history preserves every previous version of a file. Deleting a hardcoded key from the current version does not remove it from history, so a leaked key effectively has to be treated as compromised and rotated.

questions.q: In an except chain with `except requests.exceptions.Timeout`, `except requests.exceptions.HTTPError`, and `except requests.exceptions.RequestException`, why must `RequestException` come LAST?
options: Python requires exceptions to be listed alphabetically
Because it's the broadest (base) class — if it came first, it would catch everything before the more specific except blocks ever got a chance to run
It doesn't matter; order has no effect on which except block runs
RequestException can only be used as the very first except clause
questions.explain: Python checks except clauses top to bottom and runs the first match. Since RequestException is the parent of Timeout and HTTPError, placing it first would catch those errors too, so the more specific handlers would never execute.

questions.q: What is the difference between `response.text` and `response.json()`?
options: response.text returns the raw body as a string; response.json() parses that body as JSON and returns a Python dict or list
They are identical in every case
response.json() only works on GET requests, never POST
response.text requires an internet connection but response.json() does not
questions.explain: response.text gives the unparsed body as a plain string, useful for any content type. response.json() additionally parses that string as JSON, handing you a ready-to-use dict or list.

questions.q: Why does the two-`await`-in-a-row example (`await asyncio.sleep(1)` twice) still take about 2 seconds, not 1?
options: Each await fully waits for its own coroutine to finish before the next line runs — await alone doesn't create concurrency
asyncio.sleep() is broken and always takes twice as long
Python requires a minimum 2-second delay for any async function
The event loop only allows one asyncio.sleep() call per program
questions.explain: await just means "run this and pause here until it's done." Chaining two awaits back to back is still sequential — concurrency requires starting both operations before awaiting either, which is what create_task() is for.

questions.q: In the lesson's synchronous example, what is `time.sleep(1)` standing in for?
options: A real network wait — sending a request and waiting for an AI provider's response
A bug that needs to be fixed
A way to slow down the CPU on purpose for testing
A required delay before Python can import requests
questions.explain: time.sleep(1) is a simple stand-in for the real wait that happens during an actual AI API call: time spent waiting on the network and the model, not on your own code.

questions.q: What does `asyncio.gather(*coroutines)` do?
options: It runs the coroutines one after another and stops at the first one
It runs all the given coroutines concurrently and returns their results as a list, in the same order they were passed in
It merges multiple coroutine functions into a single function definition
It only works with exactly two coroutines at a time
questions.explain: asyncio.gather() starts every coroutine it's given concurrently and collects all of their results into a list once all are finished, preserving the original input order regardless of finishing order.

questions.q: What makes the "print() debugging, with intent" approach in this lesson different from scattering print statements everywhere?
options: It avoids using print() entirely in favor of logging
It requires installing a separate print-debugging library
It only works inside async functions
It uses a clear, searchable prefix (like "DEBUG:") and prints a specific targeted value instead of dumping entire objects blindly
questions.explain: The lesson's approach to print() debugging emphasizes being deliberate: a consistent prefix makes debug lines easy to find and remove later, and printing a specific value (like dict keys) is more useful than dumping an entire object.

questions.q: Why would a test like `test_divide_by_zero_raises` be considered just as important as a test checking a normal return value?
options: It confirms the code fails correctly and predictably under bad input, which is just as important as confirming correct behavior on good input
It isn't — only happy-path tests matter
It's required by Python syntax rules
It makes the test suite run faster
questions.explain: Code that silently returns a wrong value or crashes unpredictably on bad input is often worse than code that fails loudly and clearly. Testing that errors are raised correctly is a core part of making code reliable, not an afterthought.

questions.q: Why would a function like `find_user(user_id: int) -> Optional[str]` use `Optional[str]` instead of just `str`?
options: Because the function can genuinely return None (e.g. when a lookup fails), and Optional[str] documents that possibility directly in the signature
Because the function sometimes returns a number instead of a string
Optional[str] and str behave identically and the choice is arbitrary
Because the function is deprecated
questions.explain: Optional[str] is shorthand for "str or None." It's used specifically to flag that a function might return None under some condition (like a dict.get() miss), so callers know to check for it rather than being surprised later.

questions.q: Which chapter's skills does the lesson say the capstone's client-wrapper design is modeled on?
options: Chapter 2's dictionaries lesson
Chapter 3's class-based client wrapper lesson (Lesson 17)
Chapter 6's async lessons
Chapter 4's dependency conflicts lesson
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly points back to Chapter 3, Lesson 17 — writing a simple class-based client wrapper — as the pattern the capstone's API client class follows.

questions.q: Why does `parser.add_argument("prompt", help="...")` with no leading dashes make `prompt` a required argument?
options: It doesn't — all argparse arguments are optional by default
The help text is what makes it required
argparse treats an argument name without leading dashes as a required positional argument; running the script without it prints a usage message and exits automatically
It requires a separate required=True flag to work
questions.explain: In argparse, an argument name given without a leading -- or - (like "prompt") is a positional argument, which is required by default. Omit it and argparse automatically prints a usage error and exits — no extra code is needed.

questions.q: What is the next course in the AI Engineer path after Python for AI Engineering?
options: AI & ML Foundations
Git & GitHub for Software Engineers
Retrieval-Augmented Generation & Vector Databases
AI Agents
questions.explain: Per the AI Engineer path's course sequence, Git & GitHub for Software Engineers follows Python for AI Engineering — version control for exactly the kind of project just built in this capstone.
